title: Lost in the old city
paragraphs: My name is Damir Yessimov. I am eighteen years old and I come from Aktau — a city on the shore of the Caspian Sea in the west of Kazakhstan. I study Geography at WKU in Uralsk. Last spring, during our mid-semester break, I decided to travel alone to Taraz — one of the oldest cities in Kazakhstan, located in the south of the country. As a Geography student, I am fascinated by ancient places and their history. I had read about Taraz in my textbooks for years, and I wanted to see it with my own eyes.

I arrived at Taraz bus station on a Tuesday morning. The station is at the eastern edge of the city. I walked through the main doors and looked for the tourist information desk. It was in the corner of the waiting area — a small table with leaflets and a paper city map. A friendly woman gave me a map and circled three places I should visit: the Karakhan Mausoleum, the Aisha Bibi Mausoleum, and the Central Bazaar. "Start with the Karakhan Mausoleum," she said. "Walk across the park opposite the station, then turn left at the corner of Lenin Street. The mausoleum is directly in front of you — you will see it opposite the small mosque."

I walked through the park confidently. It was a peaceful park with tall poplar trees lining the path on both sides. At the end of the path, I turned left — just as the woman had told me. But after fifteen minutes of walking, I could not see any mosque or mausoleum. I walked past a primary school, a post office, and a busy market. I turned right, then left again, then straight on along a narrow lane between old apartment buildings. The street numbers went from fourteen to twenty-two and then — nothing. I was completely lost. I had the map in my hand, but the street names on the map were different from the signs on the walls of the buildings. It was confusing and a little embarrassing.

A woman was standing at the gate of her house, watering flowers in the small garden in front of her door. I stopped and asked for directions. She smiled kindly. "You have gone too far," she said. "Go back to the end of this street. At the corner, turn right. Walk past the post office — do not turn there — and continue straight on until you reach the bridge over the river. Cross the bridge and the mausoleum is directly in front of you, with the mosque on the left." She was absolutely right. In less than ten minutes, I was standing in front of the Karakhan Mausoleum — a tall, ancient brick structure that is over a thousand years old.

The Karakhan Mausoleum was extraordinary. It stood in a small open square, surrounded by low stone walls and old trees. The entrance was on the south side, facing the mosque opposite. On the left of the mausoleum, there was a small museum with photographs and historical information. On the right, there was a garden with information boards written in three languages: Kazakh, Russian, and English. Inside, the walls were decorated with beautiful geometric patterns. It was quiet and peaceful — very different from the noisy streets outside. I sat on a bench next to the museum entrance and drew a careful sketch of the building in my notebook. Then I sat there for a long time and just thought about all the history that surrounded me.

Later that afternoon, I found the Aisha Bibi Mausoleum — this time without getting lost. I followed the map carefully, making a note of each turning and each landmark I passed. I came back to the bus station as the sun was going down, tired but very content. Getting lost, I decided, was not a disaster — it was part of the adventure. I had walked through streets that no tourist guide would ever show you, past small bakeries, local schools, and private gardens. I had spoken to real people who lived there. I had seen Taraz in a way that most visitors never do. For a Geography student, every part of a city is worth exploring.

dialogue.speaker: Arman
dialogue.text: Damir! How was Taraz? Did you find the mausoleum in the end?

dialogue.speaker: Damir
dialogue.text: Yes — but only after getting completely lost for half an hour first!

dialogue.speaker: Arman
dialogue.text: You got lost? You study Geography! That is embarrassing.

dialogue.speaker: Damir
dialogue.text: The street names on my map were different from the signs on the buildings!

dialogue.speaker: Arman
dialogue.text: So how did you finally find it?

dialogue.speaker: Damir
dialogue.text: A woman at the corner of a street helped me — she told me to cross the bridge.

dialogue.speaker: Arman
dialogue.text: Was the mausoleum worth all that trouble?

dialogue.speaker: Damir
dialogue.text: Completely. Over a thousand years old, right in the middle of the city.

dialogue.speaker: Damir
dialogue.text: A museum on the left, a garden on the right, and a mosque directly opposite.

dialogue.speaker: Arman
dialogue.text: And the Aisha Bibi Mausoleum — did you get lost again?

dialogue.speaker: Damir
dialogue.text: Not this time! I followed the map properly and noted every landmark I passed.
